extracted.intended_audience: Lords and Commons; Parliamentarians; learned men; the literate public concerned with printing regulation
extracted.subtask_description: A seventeenth‑century polemical essay arguing against pre-publication licensing and censorship of books, addressed to Parliament and the educated public, laying out practical, moral, and political objections to a licensing order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing cannot prevent the spread of vice
rubrics_metrics.description: diffolute may quickl) be con- vey'd, and that evill manners are as perfei tl) learnt without books a thoufand other ways whi< h cannot be ftopt
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: evil doctrine and manners propagate by many channels besides books (oral teaching, example, customs), so licensing books will not achieve the aim of correcting manners; examples include household practices, music, pastimes, and oral traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licencers would need to be infallible to be just
rubrics_metrics.description: how fhall the licencers themfelves be confided in, unleffe we can conferr upon them, or they affume to themfelves above all others in the Land, the grace of infallibility, and uncorruptedneffe
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: For licensing to be fair it would require licencers 'above the common measure' — studious, learned, judicious — otherwise mistakes and injustice in censorship are inevitable; the text warns against trusting fallible men with such power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulating print implies regulating all amusements and social mores
rubrics_metrics.description: If we think to regulat Printing, thereby to rectifie manners, we mufl regulat all recreations and pailimes, all that is delightful] to man... No mufick mufl be heard, no fong be fet or fung... There mufl be licencing dancers, that no geflure, motion, or deportment be taught our youth but what by their allowance mail be thought honefl
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance/antipattern: The author argues that attempting to control morals by controlling printed books logically extends to absurd levels — music, dance, clothing, speech, domestic behaviour — creating impossible administrative overreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing is impracticable and will be ineffective or easily eluded
rubrics_metrics.description: Do we not fee, not once or oftner, but weekly that continu'd Court-libell againft the Parlament and City, Printed... and difpers't among us for all that licencing can doe? If then the order fhall not be vain and fruftrat... behold a new labour... ye muft repeal and profcribe all fcandalous and unlicenc't books already printed and divulg'd
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Enforcement would require massive, impractical bureaucracy (cataloguing, seizing, expurgating existing books, policing imports). Even strict systems are shown to fail in practice; censorship is readily circumvented and produces administrative burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Books often mix useful and harmful material, making simple prohibition insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: There be alfo books which are partly ufefull and excellent, partly culpable and pernicious; this work will afk as many more officials to make expurgations and expunclions
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Many works require nuanced treatment (expurgation/redaction) rather than blanket bans; censorship thus demands difficult editorial decisions and further labor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing discourages and affronts true learning and learned men
rubrics_metrics.description: I laftly proceed from the no good it can do, to the manifest hurt and caufes, inbeing nrft the greateft difcouragement and affront that can be offer'd to learning and to learned men... to difhearten utterly and difcontent... the free and ingenuous fort of fuch as evidently were born to ftudy
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: The imposition of licensing is argued to demoralize dedicated scholars who pursue learning for truth rather than lucre, discouraging intellectual effort and damaging the culture of learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing degrades authors' authority and autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: When a man writes to the world, he summons up all his reafon... if in this the moll confummat act of his fidelity and ripeneffe, no years, no induflry... can bring him to that ftate of maturity, as not to be flill miftrufted... he muft appear in Print like a punie with his guardian, and his cenfors hand on the back of his title
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Requiring an Imprimatur/guardian reduces an author's independence, undermines his authority, and subjects finished works (and later spontaneous improvements during proof) to obstruction and humiliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licencing will select only what is already 'vulgarly received', stifling innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: though a licencer fhould happ'n to be judicious more then ordnary... yet his very office, and his commiflion enjoyns him to let paffe nothing but what is vulgarly receiv'd already
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: The institution will naturally favor conservative, popularly accepted views and suppress adventurous or truth-advancing speech; this is a structural bias of censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licencing breeds arrogance, suspicion, and a low class of licencers
rubrics_metrics.description: we may eafily forefee what kind of licencers we are to expert hereafter, either ignorant, imperious, and remiffe, or bafely pecuniary... to be either ignorant or corrupt
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: The role's burdens will deter capable men and attract either lazy, authoritarian, or money‑motivated officers; this harms the quality of censorship decisions and legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial censorship often backfires by enhancing the reputation of forbidden writings
rubrics_metrics.description: the punifhing of wits enhanecs their autority... and a forbidden writing is thought to be a certain fpark of truth... a nurfmg mother to feels, but... a ftep-dame to Truth
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Suppression can make writings more influential and give persecuted authors prestige; censorship can thus amplify, rather than suppress, dangerous opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licencing insults and infantilizes the common people
rubrics_metrics.description: for if we fo jealous over them, as that we dare not truft them with an Englifh pamphlet, what doe we but cenfure them for a giddy, vitious, and ungrounded people
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Treating the laity as untrustworthy readers is demeaning and parallels systems used to oppress laity in 'Popish places'; it is politically and morally objectionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licencing will harm ministers and religious instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: it reflects to the difrepute of our Minifters... that all the Sermons,, all the Lectures preacht, printed... fhould not be armor anough againft one Qngle enchiridion, without the caftle ol Si Angelo of an Imprimatur
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Preaching and religious teaching, which rely on broad dissemination of sermons and lectures, would be undermined if every small text required licensing; this weakens public instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: A law that restrains uncertainly works equally for good and evil and is therefore frivolous
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be better done to learn that the law mufl needs be frivolous which goes to reftrain things, uncertainly and yet equally working to good, and to evill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Laws that restrict speech in vague or catch-all ways will operate on both virtuous and harmful things; such indiscriminate restraint is illegitimate and counterproductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth requires exercise and debate; censorship causes stagnation
rubrics_metrics.description: Well knows he who ufes to confider, that our faith and knowledge thrives by exercife... if her waters flow not in a perpetuall progression, they fick'n into a muddy pool of conformity and tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Open printing and disputation keep truth alive and tested; removing that circulation freezes belief into unexamined tradition and implicit faith, which is dangerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing institutionalizes a new tyranny akin to the Inquisition
rubrics_metrics.description: which I know ye abhorre to doe... the Inquifitionall rigor that hath bin executed upon books... it was that which had dampt the glory of Italian wits
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: The author warns that adopting licensing will create an inquisitorial culture (as in Italy/Spain) that suppresses free inquiry and fosters flattery and fear, harming national intellectual life.
